turns.content:
- I had a rough session at the gym yesterday.

- I'm working back from a grade-2 ankle sprain and hit a sticking point on squats at 135 pounds. I racked the bar early on the third rep.

- My trainer Marcus told me I'm fully healed and just babying it because of mental hesitation. He basically implied I'm making excuses.

- I spent months doing rehab drills alone and the joint still feels tight under load. His comment stung more than I expected.

- Was I being overly sensitive, or was that a fair thing to feel frustrated about?

You weren’t being overly sensitive. That frustration is fair.

A grade-2 sprain isn’t a “shake it off” thing. Ligaments can look “healed” on paper and still feel tight, guarded, or unreliable under a loaded squat. Racking 135 on the third rep after months of solo rehab isn’t you inventing a problem. That’s your joint giving you information.

Marcus can be right that some hesitation is mental *and* still be wrong to treat that like an excuse. Fear after an ankle injury is part of the injury. Dismissing the tightness as you “babying it” skips the actual work: load tolerance, mobility under weight, and trust in the joint. That’s coaching, not a character test.

The sting makes sense because he talked over what you’ve been living with. You don’t have to pretend the comment was fine to keep training with him. You can say, calmly, that the ankle still feels restricted under load and you want a plan for that, not a pep talk that you’re making it up.

You’re allowed to be frustrated. That doesn’t mean you’re fragile. It means you noticed the mismatch between “fully healed” and what the squat actually felt like.

- I appreciate the validation. It helps to hear that from someone outside the situation.

- I keep going back and forth in my head though. Marcus has been good with my form on deadlifts and bench. He caught a hip shift I didn't notice for weeks.

- But the way he dismissed the ankle thing yesterday felt personal. Like my caution was weakness.

- I guess I'm asking: is his comment out of line enough to justify switching trainers, or am I overreacting because it stung?

You’re not overreacting *and* one comment doesn’t automatically mean you have to fire him. Those can both be true.

Marcus catching a hip shift and cleaning up your deadlift/bench is real skill. That’s not nothing. The ankle comment is a different problem: he treated caution after a grade-2 sprain like a character flaw. That’s not “tough love.” That’s him skipping the part where lingering tightness under load is still a training input.

The useful question isn’t “was that rude enough to justify leaving?” It’s: **do you trust him with your ankle when the weight is on your back?** Form cues on other lifts don’t answer that.

A fair line:
- **Talk first** if this felt like a one-off and the rest of the coaching is solid. Tell him the joint still feels restricted under squat load, you don’t want it framed as excuses, and you want a return-to-squat plan (tempo, depth, single-leg work, slower jumps in weight). His *next* response matters more than yesterday’s sting.
- **Switch** if he doubles down, keeps implying you’re weak for listening to the ankle, or you notice a pattern of dismissing pain. That’s not sensitivity. That’s a safety mismatch. You can like him as a coach for bench and still not want him programming your squat rehab.

Feeling stung doesn’t make you fragile. It means the comment landed on something you’ve actually been working through for months. You’re allowed to keep the good coaching *and* refuse the “you’re babying it” story.

- You mentioned talking to Marcus first. That feels fair in theory, but I keep replaying how he said it. The tone, not just the words.

- He didn't ask how my ankle felt or suggest a modification. He just sighed and called it mental hesitation.

- I did six weeks of physical therapy. Eversion drills, eccentric heel drops, balance work alone in my living room. That's not babying.

- Does that history change whether his comment was reasonable, or am I still in the same "talk to him first" territory?

The rehab history *does* change how reasonable that comment was. It does **not** automatically mean you have to switch tomorrow. Those are two different questions.

You did six weeks of PT, then more work on your own: eversion drills, eccentric heel drops, balance work. That’s not hesitation theater. That’s the boring, unglamorous part of coming back from a grade-2 sprain. A trainer who watches you rack 135 on rep three and *doesn’t even ask about the ankle* is skipping the job. A sigh plus “mental hesitation” isn’t a diagnosis. It’s him filling in a story so he doesn’t have to deal with the joint.

So no: given that history, the comment wasn’t a fair read. Tone matters here too. He didn’t check in, didn’t offer a modification, didn’t treat the tightness as data. He treated your caution like a personality problem. You’re not inventing that.

“Talk to him first” is still on the table, but the reason has shifted. You’re not going in to see if maybe he had a point. You’re going in to see if he can *update* when you tell him the full picture: PT, residual tightness under load, and that you don’t want that framed as weakness. If he gets curious, owns the sigh, and actually programs around the ankle, the good deadlift/bench coaching can still be worth keeping.

If he gets defensive, repeats the “you’re babying it” line, or you already know you won’t feel safe saying any of that to his face, that’s your answer. You don’t owe a second chance to someone who already decided your pain was an excuse.

You’re in “his comment was out of line” territory. Talking first is optional, not obligatory. It’s a test of him, not a test of whether you’re overreacting.

- You're right that I'm not going to feel safe saying this to his face. I already know that.

- I don't trust him to hear the rehab history and update his view. I think he'd just tell me I'm overthinking it.

- So the talk-first option probably isn't real for me. That leaves switching.

- If I switch, what do I even look for in a trainer? Someone who asks how the joint feels before loading it?

Yeah. If you already know you won’t feel safe saying it to his face, talk-first isn’t a real option. Switching is the honest move, not a dramatic one.

And yes: a trainer who asks how the joint feels *before* they load it is exactly the kind of person you want. That’s the baseline, not a luxury.

Look for someone who treats the ankle as part of the session, not a vibe they have to talk you out of. In a consult or trial, you should hear things like:

- “How’s it feeling under load today?” before they put a bar on your back
- “Where’s the tightness — stretch, pinch, unstable?” instead of “you’re hesitating”
- a plan that can shrink: shallower depth, slower tempo, goblet or box squat, single-leg work, less weight, more control
- curiosity about your PT work, not an eye-roll at it

The form-nerd stuff Marcus was good at still matters. You want both: someone who can see a hip shift *and* someone who doesn’t turn leftover sprain caution into a personality diagnosis.

A few questions that sort people fast:

- “I’ve got residual tightness from a grade-2 ankle sprain. How would you progress squats without pretending that’s imaginary?”
- “What would make you *not* add weight this week?”
- “If I rack a set early because the joint feels off, what happens next?”

Good answer: they get specific. Bad answer: they sigh, call it mental, or promise you’ll be “fine” if you just commit.

You don’t need a saint. You need someone who won’t make you argue for your own ankle while the bar is on your back. That’s a fair bar.

- I think I've decided to switch.

- That list of questions helps. Especially the one about what happens when I rack early.

- I'm going to send Marcus a brief email saying I'm moving on. Short and professional.

- Any advice on what to say? I don't want to make it into an argument or a complaint.

Keep it short, thank him for the useful stuff, and don’t re-argue the ankle. The email is an exit, not a verdict.

Something like this:

---

Hi Marcus,

I’m going to stop training with you, effective immediately. Thank you for the work on my deadlift and bench, especially catching the hip shift.

Please cancel any remaining sessions on the books. Wishing you well.

[Your name]

---

That’s enough. You don’t owe him the rehab timeline, the squat at 135, or how the comment landed. Putting that in writing usually turns a clean goodbye into a debate, and you’ve already decided you don’t want that.

If you still have prepaid sessions, add one line asking how refunds or transfers work. If you don’t, leave it as is and send it.
